subsection: 6. A European regional case study of identity

notes.h: Structuring an essay on a regional case study
notes.b: Identity is layered: local, regional, national and European identities coexist, and each is shaped by several cultural factors. Choose one region and use only that region's facts, because a mixed answer cannot be developed in depth.
points: The cultural factors are language, religion, ethnicity (belonging to a people with a shared ancestry and culture), nationality (belonging to a nation or state), culture and shared history.

The six headings are: historical developments (physical and political boundaries), ethnicity and race, religion, music, art and festivals, the role of migration (people moving in or out of a region), and new boundaries.
Choose about four factors as the aspects of the essay, and develop each with the region’s dated facts, so that every point is backed by a specific example.

Finish with an evaluation of how the factors combine, or cut across one another, in the region. Cutting across means that two divisions do not line up, for example a language divide that does not match a religious divide.
notes.tip: The case-study essay is Higher Level only and always refers to one European region. Write about one region only, never a hybrid. Aim for about four aspects such as boundaries, language or ethnicity, religion, and culture or migration, each with dated facts, and an evaluation of how the factors combine.

notes.b: Switzerland's landscape shaped where people live and how separate its communities stayed. Mountains divided the country into valleys, while the lowland carries most of the population.
points: About 60% of Switzerland is in the Alps (Europe's great mountain range); the Jura mountains, a lower range, lie in the north-west.
Most people and cities are on the Swiss Plateau (Mittelland), the lowland between the Alps and the Jura, because the mountains are hard to settle.
The mountains isolated valleys, which helped preserve local dialects and Romansh (a small Swiss language), since communities had little contact with one another.
Switzerland is landlocked (it has no sea coast); Lake Geneva (shared with France) and Lake Constance (shared with Germany and Austria) form parts of its borders.
The Rhine and Rhône rise in the Swiss Alps, so the mountains are the source of both rivers.

notes.b: Switzerland began as a small alliance of mountain communities and grew by adding members. Its independence, neutrality and borders were later confirmed by European treaties.
points: The Federal Charter of 1 August 1291 was an alliance of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden (three founding cantons, the member states of Switzerland); 1 August is the national day.
The Confederation (a league of self-governing members) grew as further cantons joined, so it was built by agreement rather than imposed from above.
The Peace of Westphalia (1648) recognised Swiss independence from the Holy Roman Empire, the loose German-centred empire that had claimed authority over it.
The Congress of Vienna (1815) recognised Switzerland’s permanent neutrality (staying out of other countries' wars) and fixed its borders; Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel joined as cantons.

notes.b: After a short civil war, Switzerland became a federal state, one where power is shared between a central government and the cantons. Its political system gives ordinary citizens and each region a strong say.
points: The Sonderbund War of November 1847 was a short civil war in which a league (Sonderbund means separate alliance) of Catholic, conservative cantons was defeated.
The federal constitution of 1848 created the modern federal state, so it settled the dispute that had led to war; it was revised in 1874 and fully revised in 1999.
There are 26 cantons with wide powers over schools, police, taxes and churches, so local differences can be managed locally.

Direct democracy means citizens decide laws themselves: they vote in referendums (votes on a single question) several times a year, and a popular initiative (a citizens' proposal for a new law) needs 100,000 signatures.
The Federal Council (the national government) has seven members from the main parties, who govern collectively, so no one party rules alone; language regions are represented by custom.
notes.tip: The Sonderbund War was short, so give no death toll. Do not claim that all seven Federal Council members are German speakers: the language balance is a custom, not a rule.

notes.h: Switzerland: neutrality and a nation by will
notes.b: Switzerland keeps its distance from European and world organisations, and its unity does not come from one language or one ethnic group. This is why it is described as a nation by will.
points: Switzerland is not in the EU; it joined the UN only after a referendum in 2002, and it joined the Schengen area (the European zone with no routine passport checks between members) in 2008.
Willensnation means a nation formed by the will of its people rather than by a common language or ethnicity, so Swiss identity rests on shared institutions and choice.

notes.b: Switzerland has four national languages, each concentrated in particular cantons. The rule that each area has its own language keeps the system stable.
points: The main languages are German (about 62%), French (about 23%), Italian (about 8%) and Romansh (about 0.5%); people may give more than one language, so the shares do not total 100%.

There are 17 German-speaking cantons, 4 French-speaking (Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura), 1 Italian-speaking (Ticino), 3 bilingual German–French (Bern, Fribourg and Valais) and 1 trilingual (Graubünden: German, Romansh and Italian).
The territoriality principle means each canton or commune (local authority) has its own official language or languages, used in its schools and administration.
German-speaking Swiss speak Swiss German dialects (Schweizerdeutsch) in daily life but write Standard German, the written form shared with Germany.
Children learn a second national language at school, so the language groups can understand one another.
notes.tip: Use only the rounded language figures given here and do not present them as adding up to 100%, because people can give several languages.

notes.h: Switzerland: Romansh, the Röstigraben and public broadcasting
notes.b: Even the smallest language has official recognition, and the language groups have their own media. Yet the groups still vote differently, and this divide has its own nickname.
points: Romansh became a national language by referendum in 1938 and a partly official language in 1996; Rumantsch Grischun, a written standard, was created in 1982 so that the language could have one shared written form.

The Röstigraben (the “rösti ditch”, named after a potato dish) is the cultural divide between German- and French-speaking Switzerland, often visible in referendum results; it runs roughly along the River Sarine (Saane) in Fribourg.
The public broadcaster SRG SSR runs separate services in German (SRF), French (RTS), Italian (RSI) and Romansh (RTR), so each language group has its own radio and television.

notes.b: Language divides Switzerland, but it does not break it apart, because people identify first with Switzerland itself.
points: No language group wants to join its neighbouring country: the French, Italian and German speakers each identify with Switzerland rather than with France, Italy or Germany.
Shared Swiss institutions and the cantonal system allow four language groups to coexist within one state, so national identity sits above language.

notes.h: Switzerland: the Reformation and religious geography
notes.b: Switzerland was split between Protestant and Catholic cantons after the Reformation (the 16th-century movement that broke from the Catholic Church). That split still shows on the map.
points: Ulrich Zwingli led the Reformation in Zurich from 1519; John Calvin led it in Geneva from the 1530s–40s, and Geneva became known as the “Protestant Rome”.
Historically Protestant: Zurich, Bern, Basel, Geneva, Vaud and Neuchâtel, so the Protestant cantons include both German-speaking (such as Zurich) and French-speaking (such as Geneva) ones.
Historically Catholic: the central cantons (Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Zug and Unterwalden), Fribourg, Valais, Ticino and Jura, so Catholic cantons also include German- and French-speaking ones.
The Sonderbund War was a religious-political conflict between Catholic and Protestant cantons, which shows that religion once divided the country.
notes.tip: Geneva, Vaud and Neuchâtel are historically Protestant (Calvin's Geneva). Do not say the French-speaking regions are Catholic: the key point is that religion cuts across language.

notes.b: Because the religious map does not match the language map, no single division splits the country in two. This is a key reason for stability.
points: Religion cuts across language: both German- and French-speaking Switzerland contain Protestant and Catholic cantons.
There are Protestant and Catholic German speakers, and Protestant and Catholic French speakers, which reduces conflict between the language groups.
Religion in 2022: Roman Catholic about a third, Reformed (Protestant) about a fifth, no religion about a third, and Muslim about 6%, so the mix has changed since the Reformation.
notes.tip: Use religion cutting across language as your evaluation point: Protestant and Catholic cantons exist in both the German- and French-speaking areas.

notes.b: Two popular votes, one in 2009 and one in 2021, put religion-related questions to Swiss voters. The 2021 vote passed narrowly.
points: On 29 November 2009 a popular initiative banning the building of new minarets (the towers of mosques) passed with about 57.5%.
In March 2021 a ban on face coverings in public passed with about 51%; it came into force on 1 January 2025.
The minaret ban concerned the building of mosque towers, so it is an example of religion becoming a subject of a national vote; the 2021 ban was a second popular vote.

notes.h: Switzerland: music, sport and traditional customs
notes.b: Alpine traditions give Switzerland a shared national culture that does not depend on language.
points: Yodelling (singing that switches rapidly between chest and high voice) and the alphorn (a very long wooden horn) are traditional Alpine music.
Schwingen is Swiss wrestling in sawdust rings, held at Alpine festivals, so it is a sport tied to the mountain regions.
1 August is the national day, marked with bonfires and fireworks, and recalls the Federal Charter of 1291.

notes.b: Each region has its own festival, and several are recognised by UNESCO (the UN body that lists world cultural heritage). They show local identity inside the national one.
points: Basel Fasnacht is a carnival beginning at 4 a.m. on the Monday after Ash Wednesday (the “Morgestraich”); it has been on UNESCO’s intangible heritage list since 2017.
Sechseläuten in Zurich (April) features a parade of the guilds (old trade associations), and the Böögg, a snowman figure, is burned to mark the end of winter.
The Fête des Vignerons in Vevey is a winegrowers’ festival held only about four or five times a century, most recently in 2019; it has been on UNESCO’s list since 2016.

notes.h: Switzerland: arts festivals and international identity
notes.b: Switzerland's identity also draws on world-class arts events, food, and a role in international affairs, especially through Geneva.
points: The Montreux Jazz Festival has been held since 1967, the Locarno Film Festival since 1946 and Art Basel (an international art fair) since 1970.
Fondue, raclette, rösti, chocolate, Gruyère and Emmental cheese are typical foods, so food is another shared symbol such as the national day.
The International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863 by Henri Dunant, so Geneva's international role is part of Swiss identity.
Geneva hosts the UN’s European office and many international organisations, which links Swiss identity to neutrality and humanitarian work.

notes.h: Switzerland: foreign residents and cross-border workers
notes.b: Migration has made Switzerland a country with a large foreign-born population. Many workers also cross the border daily rather than live in Switzerland.
points: Foreign nationals make up about a quarter of the permanent resident population (about 27% in 2023).
The largest groups are Italians, Germans, Portuguese and French, plus large communities from Kosovo and elsewhere in former Yugoslavia, Spain and Turkey, so the foreign population is itself varied.
Most Swiss Muslims have roots in former Yugoslavia (Kosovo, Bosnia and North Macedonia) or Turkey, so migration brought Islam to Switzerland.
Almost 400,000 cross-border commuters from France, Italy and Germany work in Switzerland each day, many in Geneva, Basel and Ticino, which are cantons that border France, Germany and Italy.

notes.h: Switzerland: guest workers and free movement
notes.b: After the Second World War, Switzerland recruited foreign labour, and later it opened its labour market to the EU.
points: After 1945 many Italian guest workers (temporary workers invited to fill labour shortages) came, often on a seasonal-worker permit that restricted family reunification (bringing relatives to live with them); this restriction was abolished in 2002.
Free movement of persons with the EU has applied since 2002, under bilateral agreements (separate two-sided treaties between Switzerland and the EU).

notes.b: Immigration has repeatedly been put to the voters, with very different results over time. Switzerland was also once a country that people left.
points: The Schwarzenbach Initiative of 1970, which sought to cap the foreign population, was rejected by about 54%, so voters at that time refused a limit.
The “against mass immigration” initiative of 9 February 2014 passed with about 50.3%, a very narrow majority.
Historically, Swiss men served abroad as mercenaries (soldiers hired by foreign rulers); the Pope’s Swiss Guard, in service since 1506, is a survivor of this tradition.

notes.h: Switzerland: the canton of Jura and Moutier
notes.b: Switzerland's boundaries have changed within the country as well. The canton of Jura was created when French-speaking Catholics broke away from the canton of Bern.
points: The canton of Jura was created on 1 January 1979 after referendums from 1974, in which the French-speaking, mainly Catholic northern districts voted to leave the German-speaking, mainly Protestant canton of Bern.
The southern French-speaking districts, mainly Protestant, chose to stay in Bern, so religion as well as language shaped the new boundary.
The town of Moutier voted in 2021 to move from Bern to Jura, and the move took effect on 1 January 2026; an earlier 2017 vote was annulled and is not the decision.
notes.tip: For Moutier give the 2021 vote and the 1 January 2026 move. The earlier 2017 vote was annulled, so do not cite it as the decision.

notes.h: Switzerland: the EU and women’s suffrage
notes.b: Boundaries of identity can also be political: between Switzerland and the EU, and between those who may vote and those who may not.
points: On 6 December 1992 voters rejected joining the European Economic Area (about 50.3% No); relations with the EU since then rest on bilateral agreements, a boundary of identity between Switzerland and the EU.
Women gained the federal vote (the vote in national elections) only in 1971, so who belongs politically changed.
Appenzell Innerrhoden, the last canton, was forced by a federal court ruling to allow women to vote in cantonal matters in 1990.

notes.b: Switzerland holds together despite its diversity because its political system and its divisions work in its favour. Use these points to close the essay.
points: Federalism gives the cantons control over schools, police, taxes and churches, so diversity is managed locally.
Direct democracy and consensus government give each language and religious group a voice, so no group feels shut out.
Neutrality and wealth reduce external pressure on the federation.
Cross-cutting language and religion mean that divisions do not line up, which reduces conflict.
notes.tip: Examiners want an evaluation of how the factors combine. Explain why Switzerland is stable despite diversity, using federalism, direct democracy, neutrality and cross-cutting language and religion.

notes.b: The Balkans, the south-east European region that was once Yugoslavia, has rugged relief that made it hard to unite. Its rivers are major routes.
points: The Dinaric Alps run parallel to the Adriatic coast, and their rugged relief fragments settlement, so communities were separated by mountains.
The Danube and Sava rivers are major features, so cities such as Belgrade and Novi Sad stand on them; the Danube flows through Belgrade, where the Sava joins it, and through Novi Sad.
“Balkanisation” is a term for the break-up of a region into small, hostile states.

notes.b: Two empires ruled the region, and the line between them became a line between faiths and peoples.
points: The Ottoman Empire (a Muslim empire based in Turkey) ruled Serbia, Bosnia, Macedonia and Kosovo for centuries, from the 14th and 15th centuries.
Austria-Hungary (the Habsburg empire) ruled Slovenia and Croatia and annexed Bosnia (took it over formally) in 1908.
The Ottoman–Habsburg frontier ran through the region, and the Great Schism of 1054, the split dividing Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, ran roughly along the same line.
The Battle of Kosovo (1389) against the Ottomans is central to Serbian national memory, which is why Kosovo matters to Serbian identity.

notes.b: A killing in Bosnia set off a world war, and after it the South Slavs were joined in a single state.
points: On 28 June 1914 Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, triggering the First World War.
The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was proclaimed on 1 December 1918 and renamed Yugoslavia (“land of the South Slavs”) in 1929.

notes.h: Balkans: the Second World War and Tito’s Yugoslavia
notes.b: The Second World War left deep wounds between the peoples, and Tito's communist state tried to hold them together under one identity.
points: The Croatian fascist Ustaše state ran the Jasenovac camp, where Serbs, Jews and Roma were killed, so the war left memories of group against group.
Serbian Chetniks (Serb nationalist fighters) also killed civilians; Tito’s communist Partisans won the war, which is why he could then lead the new Yugoslavia.
Socialist Yugoslavia under Josip Broz Tito (1945–1980) had six republics: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia.
Two autonomous provinces (areas with some self-rule) lay within Serbia: Kosovo and Vojvodina; the official slogan was “brotherhood and unity”, which aimed to stop ethnic rivalry.
Tito died in May 1980.

notes.b: After Tito's death, leaders who stressed national identity gained power, and this began the break-up of Yugoslavia.
points: Slobodan Milošević rose to power in Serbia from 1987, so nationalism became a force in Serbian politics.
Kosovo’s autonomy was removed in 1989, which increased tension with its mostly Albanian population.

notes.h: Balkans: South Slavs and shared language
notes.b: The main peoples of the former Yugoslavia are closely related. Their differences are of religion, script and history, not of race.
points: The South Slav peoples are the Slovenes, Croats, Serbs, Bosniaks, Montenegrins and Macedonians; they are of similar ancestry and largely speak one language.
That language, Serbo-Croatian, is now standardised as Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian and Montenegrin; the groups mostly understand each other.
Serbs use Cyrillic (the alphabet used in Russia) as well as Latin script (the alphabet used in English); Croats use Latin.
The groups differ in religion, script and history, not in race: ethnicity is defined largely by religion.
notes.tip: Do not describe Balkan groups as different races. The groups mostly understand each other, and the differences are of script, religion and history.

notes.b: Not every group in the region is a South Slav. Census figures from Bosnia show how its population mix changed.
points: Albanians, a non-Slav people, are about nine-tenths of Kosovo’s population, so Kosovo is the main exception to the South Slav pattern.
Hungarians form a minority in Vojvodina, so this autonomous province within Serbia has a non-Slav minority too.
Bosnia’s 1991 census (population about 4.4 million) recorded Muslims (Bosniaks) at about 44%, Serbs at about 31% and Croats at about 17%.
The 2013 census (about 3.5 million) recorded Bosniaks at about 50%, Serbs at about 31% and Croats at about 15%, so the total population was smaller and the Bosniak share larger than in 1991.
Bosniaks were counted as “Muslims” (a nationality) in 1991; the term Bosniak came into general use during the war.
notes.tip: Remember that Bosniaks were counted as Muslims in 1991, and that the term Bosniak came into general use during the war.

notes.b: Religion divides the South Slavs more clearly than language does. Religious buildings show both coexistence and conflict.
points: Catholic Slovenes and Croats, Orthodox Serbs, Montenegrins and Macedonians, and Muslim Bosniaks and most Albanians (many of whom converted under the Ottomans) make up the religious groups.
Sarajevo has a mosque, a Catholic cathedral, an Orthodox cathedral and a synagogue within a short walk of each other; the Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque dates from the 1530s.
The Ferhadija Mosque in Banja Luka (16th century) was blown up by Bosnian Serb forces in 1993 and reopened in 2016 after rebuilding, which shows religious buildings were war targets.
Medjugorje, Bosnia and Herzegovina, has been a Catholic pilgrimage site (a place people travel to for religious reasons) since reported apparitions (visions) in 1981.

notes.b: When Yugoslavia broke up, the new borders did not match where each group lived, and war followed. The wars in Slovenia and Croatia came first.
points: Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991, and a ten-day war followed.
Croatia declared independence the same day; war from 1991 to 1995 pitted Croatia against Croatian Serb forces backed by the Yugoslav army.
Vukovar was besieged (surrounded and attacked) and destroyed in 1991, which makes it an example of a town ruined by the Croatian war.
In Operation Storm (August 1995) Croatia retook the Krajina (an area held by Croatian Serb forces), and about 200,000 Serbs fled.

notes.h: Balkans: the Bosnian war and ethnic cleansing
notes.b: Bosnia, where Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats lived mixed together, was at war from 1992 to 1995. Groups were forced out so that areas would become uniform.
points: The Bosnian war of 1992–95 killed about 100,000 people, and about half the population was forced from their homes.
“Ethnic cleansing” means forcing out other groups to make areas ethnically uniform.
The siege of Sarajevo by Bosnian Serb forces lasted from April 1992 to February 1996, the longest siege of a capital city in modern warfare.
Mostar’s Old Bridge (Stari Most, 1566) was destroyed by Croat forces on 9 November 1993 and rebuilt in 2004; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
In July 1995 about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed at Srebrenica by Bosnian Serb forces; international courts ruled this a genocide (the deliberate destruction of a people).
The Dayton Agreement of 1995 ended the war.
notes.tip: Give only the Bosnia death toll (about 100,000) and Srebrenica (about 8,000). Do not give a total for all the Yugoslav wars.

notes.h: Balkans: the Kosovo war and the tribunal
notes.b: The Kosovo war of 1998–99 followed the Bosnian war, and an international court later tried the leaders responsible.
points: NATO (the Western military alliance) bombed Serbia for 78 days (March–June 1999) during the Kosovo war of 1998–99.
About 800,000 Kosovo Albanians fled or were expelled during the Kosovo war.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), a UN court for war crimes, sat in The Hague from 1993 to 2017.
Milošević died in custody in 2006 before a verdict; Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić were convicted of genocide.

notes.b: Music and festivals show identity in the Balkans: some come from tradition, and some were created to oppose nationalism or war.
points: EXIT festival, held at Petrovaradin Fortress in Novi Sad, Serbia, began in 2000 as a student movement against Milošević.
The Guča Trumpet Festival in Serbia is a brass-band festival held since 1961.
The Sarajevo Film Festival was founded in 1995, during the siege, as an act of cultural defiance.
Sevdalinka (sevdah) is a traditional Bosnian love song; the kolo is a circle dance, and the Serbian kolo is on UNESCO’s list (2017).

notes.h: Balkans: sport, Eurovision and symbols of nationalism
notes.b: Sport and popular culture reflected the changing mood, from shared Yugoslav success to open rivalry.
points: Divers jump from Mostar’s Old Bridge each summer, a tradition linked to the bridge that was rebuilt after its destruction.
On 13 May 1990 fans rioted at the Dinamo Zagreb–Red Star Belgrade match in Zagreb’s Maksimir stadium; the riot is remembered as a sign of the coming war.
Yugoslavia won the Eurovision Song Contest (an international song competition) in 1989 and Serbia won in 2007; Croatia reached the football World Cup final in 2018.

notes.b: People have left the region for work since the 1960s, and young people are still leaving today.
points: West Germany signed a guest-worker agreement with Yugoslavia in 1968; many Yugoslavs also went to Austria and Switzerland, from the 1960s.
Large-scale emigration of young people is causing population decline in Serbia, Bosnia and Croatia.

notes.h: Balkans: wartime displacement and the 2015 route
notes.b: The wars forced people to move, and in 2015 the region became a transit route for refugees from elsewhere.
points: The 1990s wars displaced large numbers of people within the region and from it, making many areas ethnically uniform.
In 2015 hundreds of thousands of refugees crossed North Macedonia and Serbia on the Western Balkans route (the overland path towards northern Europe).
Hungary built a border fence in 2015 to block the route.

notes.b: The break-up of Yugoslavia produced a series of new states, each with new boundaries, over about fifteen years.
points: Slovenia and Croatia became independent in 1991; Macedonia in 1991, renamed North Macedonia in 2019 after an agreement with Greece; and Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992.
The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) was formed in 1992 and renamed Serbia and Montenegro in 2003; Montenegro became independent in 2006.

notes.h: Balkans: Kosovo and the Dayton structure
notes.b: Two cases show that the new boundaries are still disputed or divided: Kosovo, which is only partly recognised, and Bosnia, which is split into two parts.
points: Kosovo declared independence on 17 February 2008; Serbia does not recognise it.
Over 100 states recognise Kosovo, including Ireland, but five EU states (Spain, Greece, Cyprus, Romania and Slovakia) do not.
Under the Dayton Agreement, Bosnia and Herzegovina is divided into the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, with a three-member presidency (Bosniak, Croat and Serb).
Brčko District is a separate self-governing unit since 2000.

notes.b: The EU offers the region a new kind of boundary: membership of a union with open borders.
points: Slovenia joined the EU in 2004 and Croatia in 2013; Croatia adopted the euro and joined Schengen (the area with no routine passport checks) in 2023.
Montenegro, Serbia, North Macedonia, Albania and Bosnia and Herzegovina are candidates for EU membership (December 2022).

notes.b: The Balkans case shows how boundaries and identity can pull against each other. Use these points to close the essay.
points: Boundaries drawn along the old republic lines left large minorities on the wrong side, so many people lived in a state dominated by another group.
The Dayton structure ended the war but fixed ethnic divisions in place.
EU accession (joining the EU) is a hoped-for softening of borders, which would reduce the importance of the boundaries that divide the region.
notes.tip: Examiners want an evaluation of how the factors combine. Show that the boundaries, religion and ethnicity reinforced one another in this region.

notes.b: The Celtic regions share a history of language survival on the edge of Europe. They split into two branches of Celtic language.
points: The six Celtic regions usually counted are Ireland, Scotland, the Isle of Man, Wales, Cornwall and Brittany, on Europe’s Atlantic fringe.
The Goidelic languages are Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Manx; the Brythonic languages are Welsh, Cornish and Breton.
Celtic peoples were pushed west by the Romans and the Anglo-Saxons.
Britons migrated from south-west Britain to Armorica (which gave Brittany its name) in the 5th and 6th centuries, as Anglo-Saxons settled eastern Britain.
Peripheral (far from the centre), mountainous or coastal locations helped the languages survive.
Manx’s last native speaker died in 1974, and Cornish’s last traditional speaker died in 1777; both languages have since been revived. There is more on this in Language as a cultural indicator.

notes.h: Wales: conquest and the boundary with England
notes.b: Wales has a long-standing border with England, drawn by early earthworks and strengthened by conquest and law.
points: Offa’s Dyke is an 8th-century earthwork (a bank and ditch) along much of the Wales–England border.
Edward I conquered Wales in 1282–83, and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, the last native Prince of Wales, was killed in 1282, so Welsh rule by its own princes ended.
Edward I built castles, such as Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech and Beaumaris, to hold the conquered land; Beaumaris has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986.
The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542 annexed Wales to England; the border with England has remained unchanged since.

notes.b: Devolution means that a national parliament passes some powers to a regional body. In Wales, the border stayed the same while self-government grew.
points: In the devolution referendum of 18 September 1997 about 50.3% voted Yes, a very narrow majority.
The National Assembly for Wales opened in 1999, was renamed the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) in 2020, and is enlarged to 96 members from the 2026 election.
Wales has about 3.1 million people (Census 2021); its border with England is unchanged, but its political powers have grown.
notes.tip: The 1997 referendum passed by about 50.3%, very narrowly. Do not confuse it with the 1979 referendum, and do not state the Senedd's 2026 election results.

notes.b: The Welsh language is the core of Welsh identity, and its strength varies sharply from place to place.
points: Census 2021 recorded about 538,000 people (17.8%) who could speak Welsh.
Welsh speaking is highest in Gwynedd (about 64%) and Anglesey (over half), and lowest in the industrial south-east.
The north-west heartland is Y Fro Gymraeg, and the south-east is English-speaking.
Language policy includes the Welsh Language Measure 2011, S4C (the Welsh-language television channel) from 1982 and Cymraeg 2050. There is more on this in Language as a cultural indicator.

notes.b: Religion in Wales was closely tied to language: Nonconformist chapels, not the Anglican church, were the centre of Welsh life in the 19th century.
points: The 1851 religious census showed that most worshippers in Wales attended Nonconformist chapels (Protestant churches outside the Church of England: Methodist, Baptist and Independent) rather than the Anglican church.
Chapels were centres of Welsh-language education, singing and community life.
The Church in Wales was disestablished (separated from state support) in 1920, and chapel-going has declined since.

notes.b: Welsh festivals and music are held in Welsh and keep the language and its traditions alive.
points: The National Eisteddfod of Wales is a week-long festival of poetry, music and literature held entirely in Welsh, alternating between north and south Wales.
The Gorsedd of Bards holds ceremonies at the Eisteddfod, such as the chairing of the bard (the honouring of the winning poet).
The Urdd Gobaith Cymru (Welsh youth movement, 1922) holds its own Eisteddfod, one of Europe’s largest youth festivals.
Male voice choirs grew in the mining valleys, so they reflect the industrial communities of south Wales, and the harp is a traditional Welsh instrument.

notes.h: Wales: sport, national symbols and food
notes.b: Sport, symbols, an anthem and food all give the Welsh a shared national culture.
points: The Welsh Rugby Union was founded in 1881; the Principality Stadium in Cardiff opened in 1999 as the Millennium Stadium.
St David’s Day, 1 March, is the national day, so it is the one date when Welsh identity is celebrated nationwide.
The anthem “Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau” (“Land of My Fathers”) was written in 1856.
Symbols include the red dragon (Y Ddraig Goch), the daffodil and the leek.
Foods include cawl (stew), Welsh cakes and bara brith.

notes.b: Migration has both weakened and spread Welsh culture. Workers came in during industrialisation, Welsh people left for new lands, and today incomers raise tensions in rural areas.
points: 19th-century coal and iron industries drew English and Irish workers into south Wales, spreading English there.
Welsh settlers sailed on the Mimosa in 1865 to found a colony in Chubut, Patagonia, Argentina, where some Welsh is still spoken.
A campaign of arson attacks on English-owned holiday homes, attributed to Meibion Glyndŵr, began in 1979.
English retirees and second-home owners have moved into rural Welsh-speaking areas, while young Welsh speakers have moved out.
From April 2023 Welsh councils may charge up to a 300% council-tax premium on second homes, a response to second-home ownership.
Newer immigrant communities live in Cardiff, so migration continues to make Wales more varied.

notes.h: Brittany: union with France and centralisation
notes.b: Brittany is the second Celtic region. Its link with France led to strong pressure to use French, and the Breton language declined.
points: Brittany was united with France in 1532.
After the Revolution of 1789 the provinces were abolished and France was governed centrally through departments (the standard units of local government).
French was promoted as the only language of the Republic, and the Breton language declined as a result.
Article 2 of the French Constitution and the Diwan schools from 1977 are part of the language policy. There is more on this in Language as a cultural indicator.

notes.b: Brittany's boundary is itself disputed, because a wartime decision removed one of its historic cities.
points: In 1941 the Vichy government (the French government that cooperated with Nazi Germany) separated Loire-Atlantique, including Nantes, the historic seat of the Dukes of Brittany, from the region.
Nantes is outside the official Brittany region, and campaigners still seek its reunification.
The 2016 regional reform left Brittany’s boundary unchanged.
notes.tip: Nantes is outside the official Brittany region. Say that campaigners still seek its reunification, and do not give Breton speaker numbers.

notes.b: Catholic tradition and a lively music revival define Breton culture today.
points: Catholic pardons are processions and pilgrimages to local saints.
Bagadoù (pipe bands), the biniou (bagpipe) and the bombarde (oboe) are traditional Breton instruments.
The fest-noz, a night dance festival, is on UNESCO’s list since 2012.
The harpist Alan Stivell led a Breton music revival from the 1970s, so traditional music was brought back to a wide audience.
The Festival Interceltique de Lorient has been held every August since 1971.

notes.b: Costume, food and a flag give Brittany visible symbols of its separate identity within France.
points: The tall lace coiffe (headdress) of the Bigouden area is the best-known Breton costume.
Crêpes and galettes (made from buckwheat), and cider, are typical Breton foods.
The Gwenn-ha-Du flag, black and white, was designed in 1923, so it is a modern symbol of Breton identity.

notes.b: The Celtic regions are linked by shared music and by cooperation to protect their languages.
points: The Festival Interceltique de Lorient, held in Brittany, brings musicians from the Celtic regions together.
Irish and Welsh cooperation on language, and EU support for minority languages, link the Celtic regions in their efforts to preserve their languages.

notes.h: Belgium: physical landscape and the language border
notes.b: Belgium's main division is cultural, not physical. Its history shows how language became tied to power.
points: Belgium is mostly low and flat, and the language border crosses open country: it is cultural, not physical.
Belgium became independent in 1830 after a revolt that began after a performance of the opera “La Muette de Portici” in Brussels on 25 August 1830.
French was long the language of government, courts, the army and universities, which left Dutch speakers at a disadvantage.
The language border was fixed by laws of 1962 and 1963.

notes.b: Belgium responded to its language divide by sharing power between regions and communities, a process of federalisation (turning a central state into a federal one).
points: The first state reform came in 1970, so the move towards federalism began more than twenty years before 1993.
Belgium became a federal state in 1993, with three regions (Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital) and three communities (Flemish, French and German-speaking).
The language divide is an example of cultural regions (areas defined by a shared language or culture). There is more on this in Cultural regions.

notes.b: Belgium has two main language groups, the Dutch-speaking Flemings and the French-speaking Walloons, with a bilingual capital between them.
points: Belgium’s population is about 11.8 million (2024): Flanders about 6.8 million, Wallonia about 3.7 million and Brussels-Capital about 1.2 million.
Dutch speakers are about 6 in 10 and French speakers about 4 in 10; the German-speaking Community in the east, around Eupen, has fewer than 80,000 people.
Brussels lies inside Flanders geographically but is its own region; it is officially bilingual, but mostly French-speaking in practice.
notes.tip: Brussels is inside Flanders geographically but is its own region: bilingual officially, mostly French-speaking in practice. Do not use an 85% French-speaking figure.

notes.h: Belgium: the Leuven split and political divisions
notes.b: The language divide runs through universities, parties and media, so the two communities live largely separate public lives.
points: The Catholic University of Leuven split in 1968; its French-speaking section moved to Louvain-la-Neuve in Wallonia.
Belgium has no nationwide parties; parties, media and schools are separate by language.
Belgium went 541 days without a new government in 2010–11, which shows how hard it is to agree between the two sides.
The Flemish nationalist N-VA has been the largest party since 2010; its leader, Bart De Wever, became Prime Minister in February 2025.

notes.b: Unlike in many divided regions, religion in Belgium did not add to the language divide.
points: Belgium is traditionally Catholic in both Flanders and Wallonia, so religion did not reinforce the language divide.
Historic conflicts between Catholics and liberals were fought over schools; secularisation (the decline of religion in public life) has since reduced religious practice.
Islam grew through Moroccan and Turkish migration.

notes.b: Belgian culture includes famous Flemish art, a comic-strip tradition and festivals, and some events express the identity of one language community.
points: The Ghent Altarpiece by Jan van Eyck was completed in 1432 and is in St Bavo’s Cathedral, Ghent.
Pieter Bruegel the Elder and Peter Paul Rubens (Antwerp) are Flemish painters, so Flanders has the older tradition of famous art, such as van Eyck's altarpiece.
Hergé (Georges Remi) created Tintin in 1929, so Belgium has a strong comic-strip tradition.
The Carnival of Binche in Wallonia features the Gilles in costumes and wax masks; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003.
Tomorrowland, an electronic music festival in Boom (Flanders), has been held since 2005.
11 July is the Flemish Community holiday, marking the Battle of the Golden Spurs (1302), when Flemish militias defeated French knights.

notes.b: Food and drink are shared symbols of Belgium that both language groups claim.
points: Belgian beer culture was added to UNESCO’s list in 2016, so it is recognised as heritage worth protecting.
Chocolate, frites and waffles are national symbols.

notes.h: Belgium: migration from Italy, Morocco and Turkey
notes.b: Labour migration from southern Europe, Morocco and Turkey made Belgium, and especially Brussels, ethnically diverse.
points: A 1946 agreement with Italy sent Italian workers to Belgian coal mines in exchange for coal.
The Marcinelle mining disaster on 8 August 1956 killed 262 miners, 136 of them Italian, so it shows how much of the dangerous mine work migrants did.
Labour agreements with Morocco and Turkey were made in 1964.
Brussels hosts the main EU institutions and NATO’s headquarters, so it is one of Europe’s most international cities.
On 22 March 2016 Islamic State suicide bombings at Brussels Airport and Maalbeek metro station killed 32 people, which exposed tensions around migration and security.

notes.b: Money and power moved from Wallonia to Flanders, and this fed the Flemish demand for more self-rule.
points: Wallonia’s coal and steel industry, in Liège, Charleroi and the Sambre–Meuse valley, declined.
Flanders grew through the port of Antwerp, Europe’s second-largest port, and modern industry, so its economy became the stronger of the two.
This reversed the historic balance of wealth and power between the two regions, feeding Flemish nationalism.

notes.b: Belgium's internal boundaries are the ones that shape identity today, and they are still debated.
points: The language border, the federal regions and Brussels’ position as an enclave (an area surrounded by another region) are the boundaries that shape identity today.
Debate continues over further devolution or separation. There is more on the present-day politics in The complexity of regions (i), and on the boundary changes in The complexity of regions (ii).

keyTerms.definition: A person’s or group’s sense of who they are and where they belong, shaped by several cultural factors at once.
A nation formed by the will of its people rather than by a common language, religion or ethnicity, as in Switzerland.
The Swiss rule that each canton or commune has its own official language or languages, used in its schools and administration.
The cultural divide between German- and French-speaking Switzerland, often visible in referendum results.
The break-up of a region into small, hostile states.
Forcing out other groups to make an area ethnically uniform.
The 1995 agreement that ended the Bosnian war and divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities with a three-member presidency.
A traditional Bosnian love song, also called sevdah.
The Gorsedd of Bards, which holds ceremonies at the National Eisteddfod of Wales, including the chairing of the bard.
The transfer of powers from a central government to regional parliaments or assemblies, as in Wales in 1999.
A Breton night dance festival, on UNESCO’s list since 2012.
A Breton Catholic procession or pilgrimage to a local saint.
The tall lace headdress worn in the Bigouden area of Brittany.
Government in which parties share power and decisions are reached by agreement, as in Switzerland’s Federal Council.

factCards.term: Switzerland: physical geography and how it shaped identity
factCards.definition: About 60% lies in the Alps, the Jura in the north-west, and most people live on the Swiss Plateau; the Rhine and Rhône rise in the Swiss Alps; Lake Geneva and Lake Constance form borders. Mountains isolated valleys, preserving dialects and Romansh.

factCards.term: Switzerland: formation of the Confederation, 1291 to 1848
factCards.definition: Federal Charter, 1 August 1291 (Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden); independence recognised in 1648 (Westphalia); neutrality recognised in 1815 (Vienna), when Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel joined; Sonderbund War, 1847; federal constitution, 1848.

factCards.term: Switzerland's political system: cantons, direct democracy and neutrality
factCards.definition: 26 cantons run schools, police, taxes and churches; referendums several times a year (an initiative needs 100,000 signatures); a seven-member Federal Council, language regions represented by custom; not in the EU; UN only from 2002; Schengen 2008.

factCards.term: Switzerland's languages: shares and the canton pattern
factCards.definition: German about 62%, French about 23%, Italian about 8%, Romansh about 0.5%. 17 German-speaking cantons; 4 French (Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel, Jura); 1 Italian (Ticino); 3 bilingual (Bern, Fribourg, Valais); 1 trilingual (Graubünden).

factCards.term: Switzerland: how language diversity is managed
factCards.definition: Swiss German is spoken but Standard German written; Romansh a national language from 1938 (Rumantsch Grischun, 1982); the Röstigraben runs roughly along the River Sarine; SRG SSR broadcasts in all four languages; pupils learn a second national language.

factCards.term: Switzerland: religion, and how it cuts across language
factCards.definition: Reformation: Zwingli (Zurich, from 1519), Calvin (Geneva). Protestant: Zurich, Bern, Basel, Geneva, Vaud; Catholic: central cantons, Fribourg, Valais, Ticino, Jura, so both language regions mix the two. Minaret ban 2009 (about 57.5%); face-covering ban 2021.

factCards.term: Switzerland: music, festivals and symbols of identity
factCards.definition: Yodelling and the alphorn; Schwingen; national day, 1 August; Basel Fasnacht (UNESCO 2017); Zurich's Sechseläuten burns the Böögg; Fête des Vignerons, Vevey (2019); Montreux Jazz (since 1967); fondue, rösti, chocolate; Red Cross founded in Geneva, 1863.

factCards.term: Switzerland: migration and immigration referendums
factCards.definition: Foreign nationals about 27% (2023), largely Italians, Germans, Portuguese, French and people from Kosovo; post-war Italian seasonal workers; EU free movement from 2002; Schwarzenbach Initiative rejected (1970); against mass immigration passed 9 February 2014.

factCards.term: Switzerland: new boundaries and changes in who belongs
factCards.definition: Canton of Jura created 1 January 1979, after French-speaking Catholic districts voted to leave Protestant Bern; Moutier voted in 2021 and moved on 1 January 2026; EEA membership rejected, 6 December 1992 (about 50.3% No); women's federal vote only in 1971.

factCards.term: Balkans: historic frontiers and empires
factCards.definition: The Great Schism line (1054) and the Ottoman–Habsburg frontier crossed the region. Battle of Kosovo, 1389; Ottomans ruled Serbia, Bosnia, Macedonia, Kosovo; Austria-Hungary ruled Slovenia and Croatia, annexed Bosnia 1908; Sarajevo assassination, 28 June 1914.

factCards.term: Yugoslavia from 1918 to 1989: key events
factCards.definition: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, 1 December 1918, renamed Yugoslavia 1929; in the Second World War the Ustaše killed Serbs, Jews and Roma at Jasenovac and Chetniks also killed civilians; Tito (1945–1980): six republics, two provinces; Milošević rose from 1987; Kosovo's autonomy removed 1989.

factCards.term: Balkans: ethnicity, language and religion
factCards.definition: South Slavs largely share one language but differ in script (Serbs Cyrillic and Latin, Croats Latin) and faith: Catholic Slovenes, Croats; Orthodox Serbs, Montenegrins, Macedonians; Muslim Bosniaks. Non-Slav Albanians are mostly Muslim. Bosnia 1991: Muslims about 44%, Serbs 31%, Croats 17%.

factCards.term: Wars of the 1990s: Slovenia, Croatia and Kosovo
factCards.definition: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991; ten-day war in Slovenia; Croatia 1991–95: Vukovar destroyed 1991; Operation Storm (August 1995): about 200,000 Serbs fled. Kosovo 1998–99: NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days; about 800,000 Albanians fled or were expelled.

factCards.term: The Bosnian war, 1992–95: key facts
factCards.definition: About 100,000 killed; half the population forced out by ethnic cleansing; Sarajevo besieged April 1992 to February 1996; Mostar's Old Bridge destroyed 9 November 1993, rebuilt 2004; Srebrenica, July 1995: about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys killed (genocide).

factCards.term: Balkans: festivals, music and sport as identity
factCards.definition: EXIT festival, Novi Sad (2000, begun against Milošević); Guča Trumpet Festival (1961); Sarajevo Film Festival (1995, during the siege); sevdalinka; kolo (UNESCO 2017); Mostar bridge diving; Maksimir riot, 13 May 1990; Eurovision wins 1989 and 2007.

factCards.term: Balkans: the role of migration
factCards.definition: Guest-worker agreement with West Germany, 1968, plus migration to Austria and Switzerland; 1990s wars displaced millions, leaving areas ethnically uniform; 2015 refugees crossed North Macedonia and Serbia on the Western Balkans route; young people emigrate.

factCards.term: Balkans: new states and boundaries since 1991
factCards.definition: Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia 1991 (North Macedonia 2019); Bosnia 1992; Montenegro 2006; Kosovo 17 February 2008, not recognised by Serbia or five EU states. Dayton (1995): Federation and Republika Srpska, plus Brčko. EU: Slovenia 2004, Croatia 2013.

factCards.term: Celtic regions: the six regions and their language branches
factCards.definition: Goidelic: Ireland, Scotland, the Isle of Man (Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Manx). Brythonic: Wales, Cornwall, Brittany. Britons migrated to Armorica (Brittany) in the 5th–6th centuries as Anglo-Saxons settled eastern Britain; remoteness helped the Celtic languages survive.

factCards.term: Wales: history, boundary and devolution with dates
factCards.definition: Offa's Dyke (8th century); Edward I's conquest, 1282–83, and castles such as Caernarfon and Conwy; Laws in Wales Acts 1535 and 1542; devolution referendum, 18 September 1997 (about 50.3% Yes); Assembly 1999; Senedd 2020, with 96 members from 2026.

factCards.term: Wales: religion and the Nonconformist chapels
factCards.definition: The 1851 religious census showed most worshippers in Wales attended Nonconformist chapels rather than the Anglican church. Chapels were centres of Welsh-language education, singing and community life. The Church in Wales was disestablished in 1920.

factCards.term: Wales: music, festivals, sport and national symbols
factCards.definition: National Eisteddfod, in Welsh, alternating north and south; the Urdd Eisteddfod; male voice choirs; Welsh Rugby Union 1881, Principality Stadium (1999); St David's Day, 1 March; anthem Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau (1856); red dragon, daffodil, leek; cawl, Welsh cakes.

factCards.term: Wales: migration in and out, and its effect on identity
factCards.definition: 19th-century coal and iron drew English and Irish workers into south Wales, spreading English; the Mimosa took settlers to Patagonia in 1865; second-home buyers now enter Welsh-speaking areas: arson campaign from 1979; 300% council-tax premium from April 2023.

factCards.term: Brittany: boundaries, religion and culture
factCards.definition: United with France in 1532 and centralised after 1789; Loire-Atlantique (Nantes) separated in 1941; Catholic pardons; bagadoù, biniou and bombarde, fest-noz, Alan Stivell; Lorient festival since 1971; Bigouden coiffe; crêpes and cider; Gwenn-ha-Du flag (1923).

factCards.term: Belgium: history, language border and federal structure
factCards.definition: Independence 1830; French long dominant in government; language border fixed by laws of 1962 and 1963 across flat, open land; first state reform 1970; federal state 1993, with three regions (Flanders, Wallonia, Brussels-Capital) and three language communities.

factCards.term: Belgium: population and language divisions
factCards.definition: About 11.8 million (2024): Flanders 6.8 million, Wallonia 3.7 million, Brussels 1.2 million; Dutch speakers about 6 in 10; German speakers under 80,000; Leuven university split in 1968; no nationwide parties; 541 days without a government, 2010–11.

factCards.term: Belgium: religion, art and festivals
factCards.definition: Catholic in both Flanders and Wallonia, so religion did not deepen the divide; Islam grew through Moroccan and Turkish migration. Ghent Altarpiece (van Eyck, 1432); Bruegel, Rubens; Tintin (1929); Carnival of Binche; Tomorrowland; 11 July Golden Spurs holiday.

factCards.term: Belgium: migration and economic reversal
factCards.definition: Italian miners from 1946 (Marcinelle disaster, 8 August 1956: 262 died, 136 Italian); Moroccan and Turkish agreements, 1964; Brussels hosts the EU and NATO; Islamic State bombings of 22 March 2016 killed 32. Wallonia's coal and steel declined; Flanders grew via Antwerp.

questions.prompt: Identity as a concept entails a variety of cultural factors including nationality, language and religion. Examine this statement with reference to a European region that you have studied.
questions.model: Switzerland only. Nationality and political history: the 1291 Charter, the Confederation’s growth, the 1847 Sonderbund War and the 1848 constitution, and the canton of Jura created in 1979 after the 1974 referendums. Language: four national languages, the territoriality principle, Swiss German dialects with Standard German, the Röstigraben, and the rule that no language group wants to join its neighbour. Religion: the Reformation under Zwingli and Calvin, Protestant and Catholic cantons in both language areas, and the 2009 minaret ban. Festivals and migration: Basel Fasnacht, Sechseläuten, the Fête des Vignerons, foreign nationals at about 27%, and the 1970 and 2014 immigration referendums. End by explaining why language, religion and nationality cross-cut one another, which reduces conflict. About 25 to 30 significant relevant points.

questions.prompt: “Cultural identity is defined by many diverse factors.” Examine this statement with reference to a case study of a European region you have studied.
questions.model: The Balkans only. Historical boundaries: Ottoman rule in the south and east and Austro-Hungarian rule in the north and west, the 1914 assassination in Sarajevo, the 1918 kingdom and the 1929 renaming as Yugoslavia, and Tito’s six republics. Ethnicity and religion: South Slavs who share a language but differ in script, religion and history; Bosnia’s 1991 and 2013 census shares; Catholic, Orthodox and Muslim communities and the Sarajevo buildings. Conflict and new boundaries: the 1991 to 1995 wars, Vukovar, Operation Storm, Srebrenica (about 8,000 killed), the Kosovo war and independence in 2008, the Dayton structure, and EU accession for Slovenia and Croatia. Culture and migration: EXIT, the Guča festival, sevdalinka, the kolo, guest workers from 1968, and the 2015 Western Balkans route. About 25 to 30 significant relevant points.

questions.prompt: “Cultural identity is defined by many diverse factors.” Examine this statement with reference to a case study of a European region you have studied.
questions.model: Wales only, with Brittany named only for contrast in one point. History and boundaries: Offa’s Dyke, Edward I’s conquest in 1282 to 1283 and his castles, the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542, and devolution (the 1997 referendum at about 50.3% Yes, the Assembly in 1999, the Senedd in 2020). Language: about 538,000 Welsh speakers in the 2021 census (17.8%), highest in Gwynedd and lowest in the south-east. Religion: the Nonconformist chapels shown by the 1851 religious census, and the disestablishment of the Church in Wales in 1920. Music and festivals: the National Eisteddfod, the Gorsedd, the Urdd Eisteddfod, male voice choirs, the harp and rugby. Migration: the Mimosa’s 1865 voyage to Patagonia, the second-home premium from April 2023, and English and Irish in-migration in the 19th century. Brittany may be named in one point only for contrast, for example its 1532 union with France. About 25 to 30 significant relevant points.
